brace.e: From Middle English brace, from Old French brace (“arm”), from Latin bracchia, the nominative and accusative plural of bracchium (“arm”).
brace.g: A curved instrument or handle of iron or wood, for holding and turning bits, etc.; a bitstock.

bracelet.e: From Old French bracelet, diminutive form of bras (“arm”).
bracelet.g: A band or chain worn around the wrist as jewelry/jewellery or an ornament.

braid.e: From Middle English braiden, breided, bræiden, from Old English breġdan (“to move quickly, pull, shake, swing, throw (wrestling), draw (sword), drag; bend, weave, braid, knit, join together; change color, vary, be transformed; bind, knot; move, be pulled; flash”), from Proto-West Germanic *bregdan.
braid.g: To make a sudden movement with, to jerk.

braid.e: From Middle English brede, bræd, bred, from Old English bred (“board, plank, tablet, table”), from Proto-West Germanic *bred, from Proto-Germanic *bredą (“board, plank”), e-grade byform of *burdą (“board, plank”).
braid.g: A shelf or board for holding objects.

bramble.e: From Middle English brembel, from Old English bræmbel, from earlier brǣmel, brēmel, from dialectal Proto-West Germanic *brāmil, diminutive of *brām (English broom).
bramble.g: Any of many closely related thorny plants in the genus Rubus including the blackberry and likely not including the raspberry proper.

branch.e: From Middle English branche, braunche, bronche, from Old French branche, branke, from Late Latin branca (“footprint”, later also “paw, claw”) (whence Middle High German pranke, German Pranke (“paw”)), of unknown origin. Perhaps of Celtic origin, from a hypothetical Gaulish *vranca, from Proto-Indo-European *wrónk-eh₂.
branch.g: The woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing.

brand.e: From Middle English brand, from Old English brand (“fire; flame; burning; torch; sword”), from Proto-West Germanic *brand, from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“flame; flaming; fire-brand; torch; sword”), derived from Proto-Germanic *brinnaną (“to burn”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil; brew”).
brand.g: A mark or scar made by burning with a hot iron, especially to mark cattle or to classify the contents of a cask.

brandish.e: From Middle English braundischen, from Old French brandiss-, stem of brandir (“to flourish a sword”), from Frankish *brandijan, from Frankish *brand (“firebrand; sword”), from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“fire; flame; sword”), whence Old English brand (“firebrand; torch”); equivalent to brand + -ish.
brandish.g: To move or swing a weapon back and forth, particularly if demonstrating anger, threat or skill.

brass.e: From Middle English bras, bres, from Old English bræs (“brass, bronze”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps representing a backformation from Proto-Germanic *brasnaz (“brazen”), from or related to *brasō (“fire, pyre”). French braser ("to solder"; > English braise) from the same Germanic root. In the military sense an ellipsis of the brass hats.
brass.g: A metallic alloy of copper and zinc used in many industrial and plumbing applications.

brass.e: From Portuguese braça and Spanish braza, from Old Galician-Portuguese and Old Spanish braça, from Latin brachia, variant of bracchium (“arm, cubit”), from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn, “upper arm”).
brass.g: Synonym of brace, a traditional unit of measure equivalent to a fathom (6 feet) or about 1.6 m, especially as the Spanish braza and Portugue

brave.e: From Middle French brave, borrowed from Italian bravo, itself of uncertain origin (see there).
brave.g: Strong in the face of fear; courageous.

brave.e: From Middle French braver, from brave.
brave.g: To encounter or withstand with courage and fortitude, to defy, to provoke.

bravery.e: Borrowed from Middle French braverie, from braver (“to brave”), or Italian braveria, from bravare (“to brave”). By surface analysis, brave + -ery.

brawl.e: It may be cognate with Danish bralle (“to chatter, jabber”), Dutch brallen (“to boast”), Low German brallen (“to brag”), Middle High German prālen (“to boast, flaunt”) (modern German prahlen (“to boast, flaunt, vaunt”)).
brawl.g: A disorderly argument or fight, usually with a large number of people involved.

brawl.e: Possibly from French branler (“to shake”), from Old French brandeler (“to shake, wave; to agitate”), from brand, branc (“blade of a sword”), from Vulgar Latin *brandus (“firebrand; flaming sword; sword”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenu- (“to burn”).
brawl.g: To move to and fro, to quiver, to shake.

brawler.e: From Middle English brawler, brawlere, equivalent to brawl + -er.
brawler.g: One who brawls, engages in noisy, unseemly fights.

bray.e: Alternatively, the word could be from a Germanic source, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”), and cognate with frangere (“to break, shatter”).
bray.g: Of an animal (now chiefly of animals related to the ass or donkey, and the camel): to make its cry.

bray.e: From Middle English brayen (“to break or crush into pieces”), from Anglo-Norman breier, Old French breie, breier, broiier (modern French broyer (“to crush, grind”)), possibly from Frankish *brekan (“to break”), from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”); thus making the English word a doublet of break.
bray.g: To crush or pound, especially using a pestle and mortar.

brazen.e: From Middle English brasen, from Old English bræsen (“brazen, of brass”); equivalent to brass + -en (compare golden, wooden, etc.). The word originally meant “of brass”.

breach.e: From Middle English breche, from Old English bryċe (“fracture, breach”) and brǣċ (“breach, breaking, destruction”), from Proto-West Germanic *bruki, from Proto-Germanic *brukiz (“breach, fissure”) and *brēkō (“breaking”).
breach.g: A gap or opening made by breaking or battering, as in a wall, fortification or levee / embankment; the space between the parts of a solid bo

bread.e: From Middle English bred, breed, from Old English brēad (“fragment, bit, morsel, crumb", also "bread”), from Proto-West Germanic *braud, from Proto-Germanic *braudą (“bread”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerw-, *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil; to brew”), from *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”). Alternatively.
bread.g: A foodstuff made by baking dough made from cereals.

bread.e: From Middle English brede (“breadth, width, extent”), from Old English brǣdu (“breadth, width, extent”), from Proto-Germanic *braidį̄ (“breadth”).

breadth.e: From Middle English bredthe, alteration (due to nouns ending in -th: length, strength, wrength, etc.) of brede ("breadth"; see bread). Equivalent to broad + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
breadth.g: The extent or measure of how broad or wide something is; width.

break.e: From Middle English breken, from Old English brecan (“to break”), from Proto-West Germanic *brekan, from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”). The modern pronunciation shows an irregular change of Early Modern English /ɛː/ to /eɪ/ in the standard language.
break.g: To separate into two or more pieces, to fracture or crack, by a process that cannot easily be reversed for reassembly.

break.e: Clipping of breakdown (the percussion break of songs chosen by a DJ for use in hip-hop music) and see also breakdancing.
break.g: A section of extended repetition of the percussion break to a song, created by a hip-hop DJ as rhythmic dance music.

breaker.e: From Middle English breker, brekere, equivalent to break + -er.

breaker.g: A small cask of liquid kept permanently in a ship’s boat in case of shipwreck.

breakfast.e: From Middle English brekefast, brekefaste, equivalent to break + fast (literally, "to end the nightly fast"), likely a variant of Old English fæstenbryċe, (literally, "fast-breach").
breakfast.g: The first meal of the day, usually eaten in the morning.

breast.e: From Middle English brest, from Old English brēost, from Proto-West Germanic *breust, from Proto-Germanic *breustą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to swell”).
breast.g: Either of the two organs on the front of a female human's chest, which contain the mammary glands; also the analogous organs in males.

breastplate.e: From Middle English brestplate, equivalent to breast + plate.
breastplate.g: A piece of armor that covers the chest.

breath.e: From Middle English breeth, breth, from Old English brǣþ (“odor, scent, stink, exhalation, vapor”), from Proto-West Germanic *brāþi (“vapour, waft, exhalation, breath”) (compare German Brodem (“haze, vapor; breath”), of a different but related formation).
breath.g: The act or process of breathing.

breathe.e: From Middle English brethen (“to breathe, blow, exhale, odour”), derived from Middle English breth (“breath”). Eclipsed Middle English ethien and orðiæn, from Old English ēþian and orþian (“to breathe”); as well as Middle English anden, onden, from Old Norse anda (“to breathe”).
breathe.g: To draw air into (inhale), and expel air from (exhale), the lungs in order to extract oxygen and excrete waste gases.

breathed.g: Having a specified kind of breath.

bred.e: From Middle English bred, from Old English bred (“board, plank, tablet, table”).
bred.g: Alternative form of braid (“board, shelf, plank”).

breeches.e: From Middle English breches, brechen pl, a variant of Middle English breche, brech, brek (“breeches”), from Old English brēċ (“underpants”), the plural of brōc (“legging, buttocks”), from Proto-West Germanic *brōk, from Proto-Germanic *brōks (“crotch, legging, trousers”).
breeches.g: A garment worn by men, covering the hips and thighs; smallclothes.

breed.e: From Middle English breden, from Old English brēdan, from Proto-Germanic *brōdijaną (“to brood”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₁- (“warm”).
breed.g: To produce offspring sexually; to bear young.

breeder.g: A person who breeds plants or animals (professionally).

breeding.e: From Middle English bredyng, bredynge, from Old English *brēdende, from Proto-Germanic *brōdijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *brōdijaną (“to brood; breed”), equivalent to breed + -ing.
breeding.g: Of, relating to or used for breeding.

breeze.e: From the earlier (nautical) term brise, brize (“breeze”), from Middle English brees (“wind”). Ultimate origin obscure. Variously supposed to derive from a Germanic source like Saterland Frisian Briese (“breeze”), West Frisian brys (“a cool wind”), Dutch bries (“breeze”), early Dutch brysen (“to blow cool and fresh”), or from Spanish brisa (“northeast wind”).

From Middle English brese, from Old English brēosa, variant of Old English brimsa (“gadfly”), from Proto-Germanic *bremusī (“gadfly”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerem- (“to make a noise, buzz, hum”). Related also to Middle English brimse (“gadfly”), French brize (“gadfly”), Old English bremman (“to rage, roar”), Latin fremō (“roar, snort, growl, grumble”).
breeze.g: A gadfly; a horsefly; a strong-bodied dipterous insect of the family Tabanidae.

brethren.e: From Early Modern English brethren, plural of brother, from Middle English bretheren, from Middle English brethere, brether + -en (plural ending). Ultimately from Old English brōþor, brōþru (“brothers, brethren”), influenced by Old English brēþer, dative singular of brōþor (“brother”). Equivalent to brother + -en (plural ending).
brethren.g: The body of members, especially of a fraternal, religious or military order.

bribe.e: From Middle English bribe, from Old French briber (“go begging”), from the noun bribe (“a gift”).
bribe.g: Something (usually money) given in exchange for influence or as an inducement to breaking the law.

brick.e: From Late Middle English brik, bryke, bricke, from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bricke ("cracked or broken brick; tile-stone"; modern Dutch brik), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *brekan (“to break”), whence also Old French briche and French brique (“brick”).
brick.g: A hardened rectangular block of mud, clay etc., used for building.

brickkiln.g: A kiln in which bricks are baked.

bridal.e: From Middle English bridale, from Old English brȳdealo (“wedding ale; wedding feast”). The attributive usage was strengthened by association with bride + -al.
bridal.g: A wedding feast or festival; a wedding.

bride.e: From Middle English bride, from Old English brȳd (“bride”), from Proto-West Germanic *brūdi, from Proto-Germanic *brūdiz (“bride”).
bride.g: A woman in the context of her own wedding; one who is going to marry or has just been married.
an individual loop or other device connecting the patterns in lacework

bridegroom.e: From Middle English brydgrome, bridegome, from Old English brȳdguma, from Proto-Germanic *brūdigumô; equivalent to Old English brȳd (“bride”) + guma (“man”). Altered by folk etymology to end with groom, with it re-analyzed as or influenced by grom, grome (“attendant”), as guma was obsolete.
bridegroom.g: A man in the context of his own wedding; one who is going to marry or has just been married.

bridle.e: From Middle English bridel, from Old English brīdel, from Proto-West Germanic *brigdil, from Proto-Germanic *brigdilaz (“strap, rein”), equivalent to braid + -le.
bridle.g: The headgear with which a horse is directed and which carries a bit and reins.

brief.e: From Middle English breef, breve, bref, from Old French brief, bref, from Latin brevis (“short”), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (“short, brief”).

briefly.e: From Middle English breefly, breffly, brevely, brevelike, breveliche, equivalent to brief + -ly.

briefness.e: From Middle English breffnes, brevenesse, equivalent to brief + -ness.

brigandine.e: From Middle English brigandyn, brigantien, attested by 1456 (eventually displacing the slightly earlier synonym brigander), from Old French brigandine, from brigand + -ine.
brigandine.g: A coat of armor for the body, consisting of scales or plates, sometimes overlapping each other, generally of metal, sewn or riveted under or

bright.e: From Middle English brighte (“brightly; (figuratively) brilliantly, lustrously; of colour: boldly, vividly; clearly, distinctly; of voice: loudly”), from Old English breohte, beorhte (West Saxon), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *berhtaz (“bright, shining”); see further at etymology 1.
bright.g: In a bright manner; brightly, glowingly, luminously, lustrously.

bright.e: From Middle English brighten (“to illuminate; to become light, dawn; (figuratively) to cleanse, purify; to clarify, explain”), from Old English beorhtian (“to brighten, shine; to sound clearly or loudly”), probably from beorht (“bright, clear”, adjective) (see further at etymology 1) + -ian (suffix forming verbs from adjectives and nouns).
bright.g: Often followed by up: to cast light on (someone or something); to brighten, to illuminate.

brightly.e: From Middle English brightliche, from Old English beorhtlice, equivalent to bright + -ly.

brightness.e: From Middle English bryghtnes, brightnesse, from Old English beorhtnes (“brightness, splendor”), from Proto-West Germanic *berhtnassī, equivalent to bright + -ness.

brilliance.g: The quality of being exceptionally effulgent (giving off light).

brilliant.e: Borrowed from French brillant (late 17th century), present participle of the verb briller, from Italian brillare, possibly from Latin berillus, beryllus (“a beryl, gem, eyeglass”), from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”). By surface analysis, French brill(er) + -i- + -ant.

brim.e: From Northern Middle English brym, bryme (“waterbody”), from Old English brim (“sea, surf”), from Proto-Germanic *brimą (“turbulence, surge; surf, sea”), from Proto-Germanic *bremaną (“to roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrem- (“to hum, make a noise”).

brim.g: Synonym of breme (“of the sea, wind, etc.: fierce; raging; stormy, tempestuous”).

brimstone.e: From Middle English brymston, brimston, bremston, forms of brinston, brenston, bernston, from Old English brynstān (“brimstone”, literally “burn-stone”), equivalent to burn + stone. Although once a synonym for sulfur, the word is now largely restricted to poetic and Biblical usage.
brimstone.g: The sulfur of hell; hell, damnation.

bring.e: From Middle English bryngen, from Old English bringan, from Proto-West Germanic *bringan, from Proto-Germanic *bringaną (“to bring”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenk-, possibly based on *bʰer-.

bring.g: The sound of a telephone ringing.

brink.e: From Middle English brinke, brenke, from Old Norse *brenka, brekka, from Proto-Germanic *brinkǭ, *brinkaz (“hill, edge (of land)”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰren- (“to project”).
brink.g: The edge, margin, or border of a steep place, as of a precipice; a bank or edge.

bristled.e: From Middle English bristled, ibrustled, iburstled, equivalent to bristle + -ed.

brittle.e: From Middle English britel, brutel, brotel (“brittle”), from Old English *brytel, *bryttol (“brittle, fragile”, literally “prone to or tending to break”); equivalent to brit + -le.
brittle.g: Inflexible; liable to break, snap, or shatter easily under stress, pressure, or impact.

broad.e: From Middle English brood, brode, from Old English brād (“broad, flat, open, extended, spacious, wide, ample, copious”), from Proto-West Germanic *braid, from Proto-Germanic *braidaz (“broad, wide”), of uncertain origin.
Early 20th century, apparent phono-semantic matching of German Braut (“bride”, also “girlfriend”, and more generally “broad, chick”).
broad.g: A prostitute, a woman of loose morals.

broil.e: From Middle English broylen, brulen (“to broil, cook”), from Anglo-Norman bruiller, broiller (“to broil, roast”), Old French brusler, bruller (“to broil, roast, char”), a blend of two Old French verbs: bruir (“to burn”), from Frankish *brōjan (“to burn, scald”) usler (“to scorch”), from Latin ustulō (“to scorch”)
broil.g: To cook by direct, radiant heat.

broil.e: From Middle English broilen (“to quarrel, present in disorder”), from Anglo-Norman broiller (“to mix up”), from Vulgar Latin *brodiculāre (“to jumble together”) from *brodum (“broth, stew”), from Frankish *broþ (“broth”), from Proto-Germanic *bruþą (“broth”).
broil.g: To cause a rowdy disturbance; embroil.

broken.e: From Middle English broken, from Old English brocen, ġebrocen, from Proto-Germanic *brukanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”). Morphologically broke + -n.

brokenhearted.g: Grieved and disappointed, especially by the loss of a beloved person or thing, such as the end of a romantic relationship.

bronze.e: From French bronze (1511); from Italian bronzo (13th c.), of uncertain origin (q.v.). First use appears c. 1721 in the writings of Matthew Prior (for which, see citation below).
bronze.g: A naturally occurring or man-made alloy of copper, usually in combination with tin, but also with one or more other metals.

brooch.g: A piece of ornamental jewellery having a pin allowing it to be fixed to garments worn on the upper body.

brood.e: From Middle English brood, brod, from Old English brōd (“brood; foetus; breeding, hatching”), from Proto-Germanic *brōduz (“heat, breeding”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₁- (“breath, mist, vapour, steam”).
brood.g: The young of certain animals, especially a group of young birds or fowl hatched at one time by the same mother.

brook.e: From Middle English brouken (“to use, enjoy”), from Old English brūcan (“to enjoy, brook, use, possess, partake of, spend”), from Proto-West Germanic *brūkan, from Proto-Germanic *brūkaną (“to enjoy, use”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHg- (“to enjoy”).
brook.g: To bear; endure; put up with; tolerate.

brook.e: From Middle English brook, from Old English brōc (“brook; stream; torrent”), from Proto-West Germanic *brōk (“stream”).
brook.g: A body of running water smaller than a river; a small stream.

broom.e: From Middle English brom, from Old English brōm (“brushwood”), from Proto-West Germanic *brām (“bramble”) (compare Saterland Frisian Brom, West Frisian brem, Dutch braam, German Low German Braam), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrem-, from *bʰer- ‘edge’.
broom.g: A domestic utensil with fibers bound together at the end of a long handle, used for sweeping.

broth.e: From Middle English broth, from Old English broþ (“broth”), from Proto-West Germanic *broþ (“broth”), from Proto-Germanic *bruþą (“broth”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to seethe, roil, brew”). By surface analysis, brew + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
broth.g: Water in which food (meat, vegetable, etc.) has been boiled.

brother.e: From Middle English brother, broþer, from Old English brōþor, brōðer, from Proto-West Germanic *brōþer, from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr (“brother”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr (“brother”).
brother.g: Son of the same parents as another person.

brother-in-law.e: From Middle English brother-in-lawe; equivalent to brother + -in-law.
brother-in-law.g: A male relative of one's generation, separated by one degree of marriage:

brotherhood.e: From Middle English brotherhod, equivalent to brother + -hood, from earlier brotherhede, alteration (influenced by suffixes in -hood, -head) of brotherrede (“brotherhood, fraternity”), from Old English brōþorrǣden (“brotherhood, fellowship”), equivalent to brother + -red (see brotherred). Piecewise doublet of friarhood.
brotherhood.g: The state of being brothers or a brother (also figuratively).

brotherly.e: From Middle English brotherly, from Old English brōþorlīċ, from Proto-West Germanic *brōþerlīk, from Proto-Germanic *brōþērlīkaz, equivalent to brother + -ly (adjectival suffix). Piecewise doublet of friarly.
From Middle English brotherly, equivalent to brother + -ly (adverbial suffix).
brotherly.g: In the manner of a brother, as a brother, as brothers.

brow.e: From Middle English browe, from Old English brū, from Proto-West Germanic *brāwu, from Proto-Germanic *brūwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃bʰrúHs (“brow”). For noun sense 4, compare Italian piglio (“aspect, countenance”).
brow.g: The bony ridge over the eyes, upon which the eyebrows are located.

brown.e: From Middle English broun, from Old English brūn (“brown; dark; dusky”), from Proto-West Germanic *brūn, from Proto-Germanic *brūnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-.
brown.g: A colour like that of chocolate or coffee.

bruise.e: From Middle English bruisen, brusen, brosen, brisen, bresen, from a merger two words, both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to break”): Old English brȳsan, brīesan (“to bruise; crush”), from Proto-Germanic *brausijaną, *brūsijaną (“to break; crumble; crack”). Provided the word's sense.
bruise.g: To strike (a person), originally with something flat or heavy, but now specifically in such a way as to discolour the skin without breaking

bruit.e: The English word is cognate with Catalan brogir (“to roar”); Old Occitan bruir, brugir (“to roar”).
bruit.g: Hearsay, rumour; talk; (countable) an instance of this.

bruit.e: Borrowed from French bruit (“noise; report, rumour”), from Old French bruit (“noise; sounds”); see further at etymology 1.
bruit.g: An abnormal sound in the body heard on auscultation (for example, through using a stethoscope); a murmur.

brush.e: From Middle English brusshe, from Old French broisse (Modern French brosse), from Vulgar Latin *brustia, from Frankish *bursti, from Proto-Germanic *burstiz (“bristle”), or also Vulgar Latin *bruscia, from Proto-Germanic *bruskaz (“tuft, thicket, underbrush”), which could be from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrusgo-.
brush.g: An implement consisting of multiple more or less flexible bristles or other filaments attached to a handle, used for any of various purposes

brushwood.g: Branches and twigs fallen from trees and shrubs.

brutal.e: From Medieval Latin brūtālis (“savage, stupid”), from Latin brūtus (“dull, stupid”), equivalent to brute + -al.
brutal.g: Savagely violent, vicious, ruthless, or cruel, often in an unintelligent manner.

brute.e: From Middle French brut, from Old French brut, from Latin brūtus (“dull, stupid, insensible”), an Oscan loanword, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us (“heavy”).
